St. Irene the Great Martyr

Saints

St. Irene the Great Martyr

Penelope, before baptism

Period
Fourth-century hagiographic setting; sources differ about her final death
Region
Magedon, Persia; Ephesus
Titles / vocation
Great Martyr · Woman
Commemoration
May 5

Introduction

St. Irene’s published Orthodox lives recount conversion, public preaching, prolonged suffering, and many conversions. The stories honor her as a Great Martyr, while their descriptions of her final departure differ.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Venerated as Great Martyr; published accounts differ about the final death and method

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The OCA calls her Penelope, daughter of Licinius and Licinia. Her Christian tutor Apellian teaches her; Timothy baptizes her with the name St. Irene. She rejects a proposed marriage and destroys her father’s idols.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4

Life and notable events

Her father’s attempt to have horses trample her ends in his death and restoration through her prayer. Further rulers persecute her; the narrative describes preaching, imprisonment, miraculous preservation, and numerous baptisms.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 5, 7, 8, 10, 12

Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.

And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.

[2] Public-domain Bible translation · Mark 9:23–24

The longer OCA account follows successive confrontations rather than one uninterrupted trial. It names several cities and rulers and describes repeated preservation from torture. Its episodes include the pit of serpents and heated bronze oxen. These belong to the transmitted martyr narrative; their place in the story is retained without presenting them as independently verified judicial records.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 7, 8, 10, 11, 12

Death and martyrdom

The OCA relates a beheading followed by restoration to life, then an empty tomb near Ephesus. It explicitly reports conflicting final traditions: death by fire in Western martyrologies and beheading in Basil II’s Menologion.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 12, 13, 14

The GOARCH reading instead ends with peaceful repose at Ephesus in the first half of the fourth century. Two days later the grave is found open and empty. The martyr title therefore does not establish one uncontested final death method.

[3] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 423

Writings and legacy

The same Greek account remembers churches dedicated to Irene at Constantinople and her patronage of Thera. It connects the island’s common name Santorini with Saint Irene. Its concise narrative stresses steadfast faith through repeated sufferings and journeys. These are reported features of the published life, rather than independently documented travel or casualty records.

[3] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 423

The shorter GOARCH reading preserves the same central identity—Licinius’s daughter Penelope, renamed Irene at baptism—while abbreviating her journeys. It includes her father’s conversion after restoration to life and connects her preaching with numerous conversions. Its account is useful alongside the longer OCA life because readers can see both common narrative elements and different endings. The commemoration remains May 5 in the printed sources. No calculated modern civil date, reconstructed itinerary, or single harmonized death method is substituted for what those sources actually say.

[3] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 423

Chronology

  1. Baptism

    Penelope receives the name St. Irene.

    [1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 4

  2. Persecution

    Preaching continues through repeated sufferings.

    [1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 7, 10

  3. Ephesus

    GOARCH places her peaceful repose here.
